# Tobit Chapter 5 — Disagreement Log
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Date:** 2026-03-17

---

## Overview
Chapter 5 introduces the story's central dramatic irony: Raphael the angel travels with Tobias in disguise as the human Azariah. The chapter is rich in dialogue and character interaction. Ten disagreements were logged, spanning document terminology (the promissory note), the announcement of Raphael's identity to the reader, Tobit's remarkable self-description, and the preservation of Semitic idioms in Hannah's lament.

---

## Disagreement 1 — Verse 5:3: *cheirographon* (the halved document)

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "note-of-hand" |
| LOGOS | "promissory note" |
| PNEUMA | "promissory note" |

**Issue:** Greek *cheirographon* (χειρόγραφον) is literally "hand-writing" — a written bond or IOU. The torn-and-matched halves function as an authentication token.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "promissory note" — LOGOS/PNEUMA consensus. EMET's "note of hand" is archaic English.

---

## Disagreement 2 — Verse 5:4: Announcing the angel

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "he-found Raphael who-was an-angel; and he-did-not know [it]" |
| LOGOS | "he found Raphael the angel standing there — but he did not know that he was an angel" |
| PNEUMA | "there was Raphael — an angel, though Tobias had no idea" |

**Issue:** This sentence is the narrator's intrusive announcement of the book's central dramatic irony. All translators handle it differently: EMET is flatly literal; LOGOS adds "standing there" for scene-setting; PNEUMA's dash creates drama. The contrast between Tobias's ignorance and the reader's knowledge is the structural engine of chapters 5–12.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "there he found Raphael, who was an angel — but he did not know this." The dash separates revelation from irony; "did not know this" is crisper than LOGOS's full clause while more precise than PNEUMA's "had no idea."

---

## Disagreement 3 — Verse 5:8: Tobias reports his find

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "I-have-found a-man from our-brethren, of-the sons of-Israel" |
| LOGOS | "I have found a man from our own brothers, one of the sons of Israel" |
| PNEUMA | "I found someone! One of our own people, a son of Israel" |

**Issue:** PNEUMA introduces an exclamation point and colloquial "someone," breaking the chapter's measured narrative register.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS — formal, complete, appropriately dignified.

---

## Disagreement 4 — Verse 5:9: *nekros zōn* — "living dead"

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "Living-dead I-am" |
| LOGOS | "I am among the living dead" |
| PNEUMA | "I'm a living corpse" |

**Issue:** This is the chapter's most striking phrase — a Greek oxymoron: *nekros zōn* (living-dead / dead-alive). EMET preserves the inversion literally. LOGOS softens it with "among the living dead," making Tobit a member of a category rather than himself the paradox. PNEUMA's "corpse" is viscerally strong but one-sided (it drops the "living").

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "I am a living dead man" — preserves the full paradox: he is alive yet as good as dead. More direct than LOGOS; retains both poles of the oxymoron unlike PNEUMA.

---

## Disagreement 5 — Verse 5:12: Azariah's self-introduction

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "I am Azariah, son of-the great Ananias" |
| LOGOS | "I am Azariah, the son of the great Ananias, one of your own kinsmen" |
| PNEUMA | "I'm Azariah. Son of the great Ananias — one of your own kinsmen" |

**Issue:** Primarily register and punctuation. PNEUMA's fragmented sentence is slightly too casual for this formal self-introduction.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS — complete, formal, includes the kinship claim.

---

## Disagreement 6 — Verse 5:13: Nathan / Jathan

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "Jathan" (transliterating Sinaiticus *Iathān*) |
| LOGOS | "Nathan" |
| PNEUMA | "Nathan" |

**Issue:** The Sinaiticus Greek reads *Iathān* (Ἰαθάν), which EMET preserves by transliteration. LOGOS and PNEUMA normalize to "Nathan," the standard Hebrew name corresponding to this Greek form.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** "Nathan" — LOGOS/PNEUMA consensus. The English "Nathan" is the recognized form; "Jathan" would confuse readers without footnotes.

---

## Disagreement 7 — Verse 5:14: Wages comparison to Tobias

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "what-is-necessary for you just-as for my-son" |
| LOGOS | "what you need just as I provide for my own son" |
| PNEUMA | "plus expenses" |

**Issue:** PNEUMA's "plus expenses" loses the emotionally significant comparison — Tobit is treating this stranger with the same provision he gives his own son. This reveals Tobit's generous character.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS — the comparison to Tobias must be kept.

---

## Disagreement 8 — Verse 5:15: "Return whole"

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "if you-return whole" |
| LOGOS | "if you bring him back safely" |
| PNEUMA | "if you bring him back safely" |

**Issue:** Greek *hygiainon* (ὑγιαίνων) means in-health, whole, safe. EMET's "whole" is technically accurate but sounds strange in English. LOGOS and PNEUMA both use "safely," which captures the sense.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS/PNEUMA — "if you return with him safely."

---

## Disagreement 9 — Verse 5:17: "Staff of our hands"

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "Is-he-not the-staff of-our-hands" |
| LOGOS | "Is he not the staff of our hands" |
| PNEUMA | "He's the one we lean on — he's our hands and feet!" |

**Issue:** The Greek *baktēria tōn cheirōn hēmōn* (staff-of-our-hands) is a Semitic idiom for "our support / the one we rely on." LOGOS preserves it formally; PNEUMA expands and modernizes. The Semitic flavor of this phrase belongs to the story's idiom.

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS — "Is he not the staff of our hands" retains the Semitic idiom which careful readers will appreciate.

---

## Disagreement 10 — Verse 5:18: Money versus child

| Translator | Rendering |
|------------|-----------|
| EMET | "Do-not add money to-money; let-it-be as-ransom for our-child" |
| LOGOS | "Do not heap money upon money; let it serve as ransom for our child" |
| PNEUMA | "Don't put money above our child. Whatever it costs, let that money be the price for keeping him safe" |

**Issue:** PNEUMA expands to three clauses what the Greek says in two. The compression of the Greek is part of Anna's emotional directness. LOGOS's "heap" well renders the accumulative sense; "ransom" is technically precise and theologically resonant (*lytra*).

**SOPHIA's Resolution:** LOGOS — direct, complete, preserves the ransom terminology.

---

*Total disagreements logged: 10*
*— SOPHIA*
